title: Maintaining Older Tailwind Projects
subtopics: v3-to-v4 migration, but the resulting changes still require review and testing.
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of maintaining older tailwind projects.
Apply one appropriate technique to a small Tailwind CSS example.
Verify the expected result and identify a common failure mode.

content.intro: In this lesson, focus on maintaining older tailwind projects and connect it to the way Tailwind CSS generates and applies utility styles.
content.why_it_matters: Maintaining Older Tailwind Projects protects existing projects from accidental regressions when framework versions and build workflows differ.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum highlights: Reading version-specific documentation; Understanding legacy class patterns; Pinning versions when required; Evaluating compatibility requirements; Planning staged upgrades. Treat these as practical decisions rather than a list to memorize: identify the intended behavior, choose the smallest suitable utility or directive, and inspect what the browser receives.

content_blocks.title: Concepts to understand
items: v3-to-v4 migration, but the resulting changes still require review and testing.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Maintaining Older Tailwind Projects
content_blocks.code:
1. Create a migration branch and record starting package versions.
2. Follow the official Tailwind CSS upgrade guide.
3. Run the build and compare key pages and states before merging.
content_blocks.expected_output: A migration is reviewed through a successful build, visual regression checks and documented manual changes.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the example, change one decision related to maintaining older tailwind projects, then compare the outcome. In a Tailwind-enabled project, confirm the generated CSS exists; class strings alone do not make styles available without a configured build.

content_blocks.title: Version and compatibility note
content_blocks.text: This course prioritizes Tailwind CSS v4. Confirm your installed version and use its matching official guide. Snippets using v3 directives or configuration are labelled as legacy and should not be mixed blindly with v4 syntax.

content.task: Create a minimal example demonstrating maintaining older tailwind projects. Include a before/after comparison and explain why the chosen utility, variant or directive is appropriate.
task_acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate at least one decision tied to maintaining older tailwind projects.
Keep the example easy to inspect, with complete utility names.
Test the outcome and document one limitation or environment assumption.
hints: Identify which listed syllabus topic is most important to maintaining older tailwind projects.
Change one utility, token, variant or configuration setting at a time.
Inspect generated CSS and computed styles before changing unrelated code.
content.expected_output: A migration is reviewed through a successful build, visual regression checks and documented manual changes.
troubleshooting: If no style appears, verify the package, CSS import and build-tool integration before changing the HTML.
If only a state or breakpoint style fails, check the full class token, source detection, condition and computed CSS.
For a framework snippet, import the stylesheet through its supported entry point and consult the current official guide.
common_mistakes: Applying maintaining older tailwind projects without checking generated styles or browser behavior.
Mixing Tailwind v3 and v4 setup examples without a migration plan.
Treating visual appearance as a substitute for semantic markup, keyboard usability or actual component behavior.
summary: Maintaining Older Tailwind Projects is one part of a predictable utility-first styling workflow.
Keep examples small, test the built interface and use version-matched documentation.
